ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the horizontal axis from left to right is marked in sequence with the spring equinox, summer solstice, autumn equinox, winter solstice, and spring equinox; the left vertical axis represents solar altitude from small to large, and the right vertical axis represents day length, with scale marks of 0, 6, 12, 18, and 24 hours. In the figure, ①②③④ are the broken lines of the seasonal changes of noon solar altitude for the four places, and curve ⑤ represents the change in day length. Curve ⑤ is about 12 hours near the spring equinox and autumn equinox, reaches its longest near the summer solstice, and reaches its shortest near the winter solstice. Then reason: day length being longest at the summer solstice and shortest at the winter solstice indicates that the place is in the Northern Hemisphere; the noon solar altitude of the same Northern Hemisphere location usually also shows being relatively high or highest at the summer solstice and relatively low or lowest at the winter solstice. Comparing the four noon solar altitude curves ①②③④, the seasonal-change phase of place ③ is closest to curve ⑤, therefore the day-length change shown by curve ⑤ is closest to place ③.
